title: Four Shapes of the Same Care
logline: A mother's day moves between a toddler who needs feeding, a sick teenager who needs medicine, a young adult leaving for a first job, and a grown child on the phone from far away who needs nothing from her at all.

object.note: Object 6 (identity not chosen) may appear subtly, for example among Chathura's things while he travels, waits or watches, only where it sits naturally in a real moment. Never staged, never the subject.

thread_in.thread: The patient attention given to a carved face becomes care given to living ones: a mother's single day moving between children who each need something different.

thread_out.thread: A mother's care leads to the bodies of those who carry: tea-leaf baskets coming off backs at the weighing shed, and relief visible in the body underneath.

lesson.in_simple_terms: Care can take different shapes depending on who is in front of you: wishing a little one well, wanting a sick one's pain to end, being glad at a grown one's good start, and stepping back when nothing more is needed. The texts use exactly this picture of a mother to explain four kinds of goodwill.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: ළදරුවාට යහපත පැතීම, ලෙඩ වූ දරුවාගේ දුක නැති වේවා යි කැමති වීම, වැඩිහිටි දරුවාගේ දියුණුවට සතුටු වීම සහ තවත් කළ යුත්තක් නැති විට මැදහත් වීම යන සතර බ්‍රහ්මවිහාරය, මවකගේ උපමාවෙන් පොත්වල පැහැදිලි කෙරේ.
lesson.the_teaching: The four sublime abidings are loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy and equanimity. The Pradeepika explains them with the image of a mother who wants her infant to grow, her sick son to recover and her young son's good years to last, and who stays even-minded about the son busy with his own affairs; in the same way the practitioner first wishes welfare, then the removal of suffering, then gladness at success, and finally even-mindedness because nothing more remains to be done. The failure of equanimity is ignorant indifference, so stepping back is not the same as ceasing to care. The Margaya describes compassion as not wanting others to suffer just as one does not want to suffer oneself, and sympathetic joy as being glad at others' gains as at one's own.
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: Across one day the mother feeds the toddler, sits with the sick teenager through discomfort, shows quiet pride as the young adult leaves for a first job, and mostly listens on a call with the child abroad. No one names what her attention is doing; the viewer notices it changing shape hour by hour, and the phone call shows that stepping back can itself be a shape of care.
lesson.caution: This does not mean stepping back is a lack of love; the texts name cold, ignorant indifference as the failure of equanimity, not its goal.
lesson.builds_on: The sculptor's patient attention went to a carved face; here attention goes to living people and changes shape with what each one needs, gathering the gladness and care of earlier films into the four abidings.
